01.note: Three Sages give three accounts of one disaster. Shmuel says Jews fleeing a religious persecution hid in a cave and agreed that anyone could come in but no one could go out; when one man's sandal was found reversed, they thought someone had left and that the enemy was coming, and in the panic they pushed one another and killed more of their own than the enemy had. Rabbi Elai ben Elazar says they heard a sound above the cave, and Rami bar Yehezkel says they heard it behind a synagogue; each time the same deadly crush followed.
01.why: The Mishna forbids going out on Shabbat in a spiked sandal, and the Gemara asks why. These accounts explain the ban as a memorial to a disaster caused by such a sandal, and the Gemara goes on to ask why the ban applies only on Shabbat and Festivals.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who explains the ban with the story of the reversed sandal in the cave

people.name: Rabbi Elai ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who tells the version in which the hiders heard a sound above the cave

people.name: Rami bar Yeḥezkel
people.about: Sage who places the panic in a synagogue

terms.meaning: Government decrees forbidding Jewish practice; those who fled them went into hiding.
A sandal studded with nails, whose sound and prints the hiders mistook for the enemy's.

02.note: A pregnant woman went into a neighbor's house to bake in the oven there. The household dog barked at her, and her fetus was displaced. The owner told her not to be afraid, since the dog's teeth and claws had been removed. She answered: Take your kindness and throw it on the thorns; the fetus has already been displaced.
02.why: Reish Lakish has just taught that anyone who keeps a vicious dog keeps kindness out of his home, and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak adds that he casts off the fear of Heaven. This incident shows the harm even a toothless dog can do.

terms.meaning: The fright caused her to lose the pregnancy; the Gemara's comment adds that the fetus will certainly die.

03.note: Rabba bar bar Hana, quoting Rabbi Yohanan, tells of a family in Jerusalem whose daughters walked with long strides, and as a result their hymens tore. The family made ankle bands for them and hung a chain between them so their steps would be short, and the hymens no longer tore. Rabbi Yirmeya was woken by the sound of the chains and said: Correct, and Rabbi Yohanan said the same.
03.why: The Gemara is asking why a chain makes a garter count as a vessel that can become ritually impure, when the chain seems to do nothing. This account is the answer: the chain performs a real function, keeping a girl's stride short.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Sage who reports the account in Rabbi Yohanan's name

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage in whose name the account is told

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Sage woken by the voices or chains who approves the practice

terms.meaning: Only objects that count as functioning vessels can contract ritual impurity; the question is whether the chain gives the garter that status.

04.note: Shmuel's father did not let his daughters go out with strings in their ears, did not let them sleep next to each other, and made ritual baths for them in the spring month of Nisan, and in the autumn month of Tishrei laid mats on the bed of the Euphrates so they could immerse without sinking into the mud.
04.why: The Mishna has just permitted young girls to go out on Shabbat with strings in their pierced ears. The Gemara cites this father's stricter practice and then examines each of his customs in turn, starting with how he could forbid what the Mishna allows.

people.name: Shmuel’s father
people.about: Father of the Sage Shmuel, who set strict rules for his daughters

terms.meaning: A pool of water (mikveh) in which a person immerses to become ritually pure.
Hebrew months: Nisan falls in spring, after the rainy season; Tishrei falls in early autumn, after the dry summer.

05.note: Shmuel's father made a ritual bath for his daughters during the spring month of Nisan rather than letting them immerse in the Euphrates. The Gemara explains he held that the river was then swollen with rain, and that water which had fallen as rain might outweigh the river's own flowing water, so immersing there would not purify them.
05.why: The Gemara is working through the customs of Shmuel's father one by one. This one is said to support Rav's view that the Euphrates swells from rain in the Land of Israel, and to disagree with Shmuel's view that the river is fed from its own bed.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who said the Euphrates is the great witness to rain falling in the Land of Israel

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel, as seen from Babylonia.
Spring or river water purifies even while it flows; rainwater purifies only when gathered in a pool, not while flowing.

05.flag: The STORY segment is mostly the Gemara's legal explanation of the father's custom, already told in the previous story; there is little narrative event.

06.note: Rabbi Akiva held a banquet for his son. Over every cup of wine he brought, he said: Wine and life to the mouth of the Sages; life and wine to the mouth of the Sages and to the mouth of their students.
06.why: The discussion is listing practices that are or are not forbidden as superstitious 'ways of the Amorite'. The toast 'wine and life to the mouth of the Sages' is ruled permitted, and Rabbi Akiva's banquet shows a great Sage using it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who made a banquet for his son and toasted the Sages over each cup

terms.meaning: Superstitious or pagan practices the Torah forbids imitating.

07.note: Rav Dimi, arriving from the Land of Israel, reported that it was Rav Beivai's Shabbat to host the students, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi happened to come. Rav Beivai set before them a basket of fruit without sorting out the leaves and stems. Rav Dimi said he did not know whether Rav Beivai did this because he held that picking food out of waste is forbidden on Shabbat, or because he wanted to show generosity with a full basket.
07.why: The Gemara is debating how far the Shabbat ban on sorting reaches, including whether taking food out of waste is forbidden. Rav Dimi's report might have settled it, but he himself says it proves nothing, since there are two possible reasons for what Rav Beivai did.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Sage who came from the Land of Israel and reported the incident

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Sage whose turn it was to host, who served unsorted fruit

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who visited Rav Beivai on that Shabbat

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Sage who visited Rav Beivai with Rabbi Ami

terms.meaning: One of the labors forbidden on Shabbat: sorting wanted from unwanted items, such as food from waste.

08.note: Rav Beivai smeared his daughter with lime limb by limb, a little at a time, to remove her hair, and when he married her off he received four hundred zuz for her. A gentile neighbor with a daughter smeared her whole body with lime at once, and she died. He said: Rav Beivai killed my daughter. Rav Nahman commented that Rav Beivai's family drinks beer, so their daughters need lime treatment; we who do not drink beer have daughters who do not need it.
08.why: The Mishna sets the amount of lime one is liable for carrying on Shabbat by its use as a depilatory on girls, and Rav has explained that use. The story about Rav Beivai's daughter follows on that use of lime.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Sage who treated his daughter with lime gradually before her marriage

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Sage who links the need for lime to drinking beer

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred zuz was a large sum.
A caustic mineral paste spread on the skin to remove hair.

09.note: A man named Zunin came into the study hall and asked the Sages what size the stones a person may carry into the bathroom on Shabbat for wiping must be. They answered: the size of an olive, a nut, or an egg. He asked them: Should he take scales into the bathroom? The Sages took a vote and concluded that he may simply take a handful.
09.why: The Mishna has been setting minimum sizes of stones for liability on Shabbat. The story turns to how big bathroom stones moved on Shabbat must be, and a baraita (a teaching from the Mishna's era left out of the Mishna) records the same two views, from Rabbi Yosei and his son.

people.name: Zunin
people.about: Man who came into the study hall and challenged the Sages' measures

terms.meaning: Standard units of volume used in Jewish law, based on the size of an olive, a nut and an egg.

10.note: Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna were traveling by boat when a certain noblewoman asked to sit with them, and they refused. She said a spell and stopped the boat; they said something of their own and freed it. She said to them: What can I do to you, since you do not wipe yourselves with an earthenware shard, do not kill lice on your clothes, and do not pull a vegetable out of a gardener's bundle and eat it before untying it?
10.why: Rabbi Yohanan forbade wiping with an earthenware shard, and the Gemara considered whether the reason is witchcraft. When it asks what witchcraft has to do with it, this story answers: the woman names wiping with a shard as one of the openings witchcraft uses.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sage traveling on the boat who refused the woman a seat

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Sage traveling with Rav Hisda

terms.meaning: A Roman noblewoman; here one who practices witchcraft.

11.note: A heretic watched Rava so absorbed in study that he did not notice he was squeezing his fingers under his leg until they spurted blood. The heretic said: You impulsive nation, who put your mouths before your ears; you are still impulsive. You should have listened first and accepted the commands only if you could keep them. Rava answered with a verse: of us, who walk wholeheartedly, it is written, 'The integrity of the upright will guide them,' while of those who walk in deceit it says, 'The perverseness of the faithless will destroy them.'
11.why: The Sages have just praised Israel for saying 'We will do' before 'We will hear' at Sinai, a secret of the angels. The heretic mocks that very order as recklessness, and Rava defends it as wholehearted trust.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage so absorbed in study that he did not notice his fingers bleeding

terms.meaning: Someone who rejected the Sages' teachings and often argued with them.
Israel's promise at Sinai, 'We will do and we will hear', which put doing before hearing what was required.

12.note: The Sages told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that young schoolchildren had come to the study hall that day and said things not said even in the days of Joshua bin Nun. They read the letters of the Hebrew alphabet as lessons: alef bet means learn wisdom; gimmel dalet means give to the poor. The gimmel's leg reaches toward the dalet because the giver runs after the poor; the dalet's leg reaches back so the poor make themselves available; and the dalet faces away so the gift is given discreetly and the poor person is not shamed.
12.why: The discussion has been about the shapes of the letters, including Rav Hisda's teaching that the closed letters on the tablets stood by a miracle. The children's reading of each letter's shape follows on that theme.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sage to whom the Sages reported what the children said

people.name: Joshua bin Nun
people.about: Moses' successor; the Sages say not even his days produced such teachings

terms.meaning: The first four letters of the Hebrew alphabet; the children read each pair as a Hebrew phrase.

12.flag: The STORY covers only the first letters; the children's interpretations continue through the AFTER segments, so the story stops in the middle.

13.note: Shmuel and Karna, sitting by the Malka River, saw the water rising and murky. Shmuel said a great man with aching intestines was coming from the Land of Israel, and sent Karna to test him. Karna found Rav and quizzed him on why phylacteries are written only on kosher hide, why forbidden blood is red, and why circumcision is done where it is; Rav answered each from verses. Rav asked his name, and on hearing Karna, said: May a horn grow in his eyes. Shmuel then took Rav home, fed him barley bread, fried fish and beer, and did not show him the lavatory so he would have diarrhea. Rav cursed: Whoever causes me suffering, let his children not survive. And so it was.
13.why: The Gemara has just asked whether phylacteries may be written on fish skin. Karna's question about writing them only on the hide of a kosher animal, and Rav's answer from a verse, bear on that question, and the Gemara goes on to the same derivations in other teachings.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who foresaw Rav's arrival, sent Karna to test him, and then hosted him

people.name: Karna
people.about: Sage sent by Shmuel to test Rav with questions

people.name: Rav
people.about: The great man arriving from the Land of Israel, who answered Karna and cursed his host

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head; the passages are written on parchment from an animal hide.
The Land of Israel, as seen from Babylonia.
An idiom for testing someone to see whether he is a real Torah scholar.

14.note: Rav Hisda said melon juice is permitted on Shabbat but the juice of pipuim is not. Ze'iri's wife made melon juice for Hiyya bar Ashi, and he would not eat it. She said to him: I made it for your teacher, and he ate it, and you will not? The Gemara explains that Ze'iri was following his own ruling that clear wine and water may be poured through a strainer on Shabbat, since that does nothing to them; so too melon juice, drunk the way it is, involves doing nothing.
14.why: The discussion is listing foods and drinks that may or may not be taken on Shabbat when they could count as medicine. The incident shows a student holding back from a drink his own teacher allowed himself.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sage who permitted melon juice on Shabbat

people.name: Ze’iri
people.about: Sage, Hiyya bar Ashi's teacher, who ate the melon juice his wife made

people.name: Ḥiyya bar Ashi
people.about: Ze'iri's student, who refused the melon juice

terms.meaning: A kind of vegetable whose juice Rav Hisda forbade on Shabbat.
A cloth or sieve for straining dregs from wine; straining is restricted on Shabbat.

15.note: Ravina visited Rav Ashi and saw that a donkey had stepped on the back of Rav Ashi's foot, and Rav Ashi was sitting soaking it in vinegar on Shabbat. Ravina asked whether he did not hold with Rav Hillel that vinegar is not permitted. Rav Ashi answered that the back of the hand and the back of the foot are different. In another version Rav Ashi was soaking his foot in wine, and Ravina reminded him of Rava's view that even wine heals delicate people like him; Rav Ashi gave the same answer, citing Rav that such a wound is like a mortal wound, for which Shabbat may be violated.
15.why: Mar Ukva has just allowed soaking a wound in wine on Shabbat, while Rav Hillel ruled out vinegar and Rava ruled out wine for delicate people. The incident adds an exception: wounds on the back of the hand or foot are treated as dangerous.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage who visited Rav Ashi and questioned his treatment

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage whose foot was stepped on by a donkey

terms.meaning: The Sages forbade most medical treatment on Shabbat, except where life may be in danger, when Shabbat may be violated.
A Babylonian town whose people Rava called delicate.

16.note: Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami's mother treated a man who had drunk exposed water. She boiled one rose with one cup of beer and gave it to him to drink. Then she lit the oven, swept out the coals, set a brick inside, and sat him on it. Something like a green leaf came out of him.
16.why: The Gemara has just given a remedy for drinking water a snake may have poisoned: five roses cooked in five cups of beer. This woman's cure used one of each, and it worked.

people.name: Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami’s mother
people.about: Woman who treated a man who had drunk exposed water

terms.meaning: Water left uncovered, which the Sages feared a snake had drunk from and left venom in.

17.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi saw a man who had swallowed a snake. Appearing to him as a horseman, he fed him hops with salt and made him run ahead of him for three mil, and the snake came out of him in pieces; another version says Rav Shimi himself swallowed the snake and Elijah, appearing as a horseman, did this for him. In Pumbedita a Jewish official was bitten by a snake. All thirteen white donkeys in the town were torn open for the cure and found unfit, and a lion ate the last one before it could be brought. Abaye said he must have been bitten by a snake of the Rabbis, which has no cure; they confirmed he had defied Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna's ban on bringing myrtle and palm branches with bells to a wedding hall. He died.
17.why: The Gemara is listing folk remedies: hops in salt and a three-mil run for one who swallowed a snake, and a torn-open white donkey fetus for a snakebite, but only if it is not unfit. Each incident follows one of these remedies.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Sage who cured a man who swallowed a snake, or in another version was cured himself

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who in one version appeared as a horseman and cured Rav Shimi

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who explained why the official's bite could not be cured

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Bisna
people.about: Sage whose ban, made when Rav died, the official defied

terms.meaning: A distance of roughly a kilometer.
An animal with a defect that will kill it within twelve months; the remedy works only with a healthy one.
A bite sent as punishment for breaking a rule of the Sages, based on the verse 'one who breaches a fence will be bitten by a snake'.

18.note: A certain Arab sick with jaundice said to a gardener: Take my cloak and give me a row of leeks. The gardener gave him the row and he ate it. Then the Arab said: Lend me your cloak so I can sleep in it a little. He wrapped himself in it and slept, and when he grew hot and stood up, pieces fell from it bit by bit.
18.why: The Gemara is listing remedies for jaundice, ending with sharp leeks from the middle of a row. The story shows that last remedy at work, followed by the sweating cure in a wrap the discussion described earlier.

terms.meaning: An illness that turns the skin yellow; the Gemara lists many folk cures for it.

19.note: Rabbi Yirmeya was walking behind Rabbi Abbahu on Shabbat in a karmelit when his sandal strap tore. Rabbi Abbahu told him to wrap a moist reed, fit for animal fodder, around it. Another time Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef when his strap tore, and Rav Yosef told him to leave the sandal where it was. Abaye asked why his case differed from Rabbi Yirmeya's; Rav Yosef said that there the sandal would not have been safe, while here it would be. Abaye objected that the sandal was still usable, since he could switch it to the other foot, but Rav Yosef answered that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, under whose view it no longer counts as a usable item.
19.why: The Gemara has been asking when tying sandal straps on Shabbat is forbidden or permitted. These two incidents turn to a torn strap: whether the sandal may be fixed or moved, which depends on whether it still counts as a utensil.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Sage whose sandal strap tore while walking behind Rabbi Abbahu

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sage who told Rabbi Yirmeya to wrap the sandal with a reed

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage whose strap tore while standing before Rav Yosef

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who told him to leave the sandal

terms.meaning: An area such as a field or side street that is neither fully private nor fully public; the Sages restricted carrying there on Shabbat.
An object fit for use; on Shabbat one may move utensils but not broken objects that have lost that status.

20.note: Rabbi Yosei told of his father, Halafta, who visited Rabban Gamliel in Tiberias and found him at the table of Yohanan HaNazuf, reading an Aramaic translation of the book of Job. Yohanan said to him: I remember your grandfather Rabban Gamliel standing on a step on the Temple Mount when such a translation of Job was brought to him, and he told the builder to bury it under a row of bricks. Rabban Gamliel then ordered the book put away, and it was buried. Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda said they turned a tub of mortar over it; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rejected this, asking where mortar would come from on the Temple Mount, and whether one may destroy such books by hand at all.
20.why: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda disagree whether sacred books in translation may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat. Rav Huna says the Sages of old already disagreed, and Rabbi Yosei, who tells this story, rules that such books are not rescued; the Gemara then asks which Sages he disagrees with.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who tells the story about his father

people.name: Ḥalafta
people.about: Rabbi Yosei's father, who visited Rabban Gamliel

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Sage found reading a translation of Job, grandson of an earlier Rabban Gamliel

people.name: Yoḥanan HaNazuf
people.about: Host who recalled how Rabban Gamliel's grandfather had the Job translation buried

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Sage, called simply Rabbi, who rejects the mortar version

terms.meaning: A translation of a biblical book into Aramaic, the everyday language of the time.
Worn-out or unusable sacred writings are not thrown away but buried or stored away to decay on their own.
